title: The enemies within and without
hook: the prayer asks for enemies to be ended; many read them also as the five thieves inside

segments.voice: Yesterday, ichhaa, the heart's wish, and your line, stay at the feet. Today the prayer turns to something harder.

Anandpur, in the last years of the sixteen hundreds. The Tenth Guru's town sits in the hills, and the hills are full of trouble. Neighboring kings resent him. Imperial armies will later come. There will be sieges, hunger, a night when the town has to be left behind. These aren't metaphors; they're men with weapons, and they're coming. In this world, the Guru writes a prayer that asks, plainly, for enemies to be ended. It's a line people stumble over when they first read Chaupai.
screen: `ANANDPUR, IN THE HILLS.` → `REAL ARMIES, REAL SIEGES.` → `A PRAYER ABOUT ENEMIES.`

segments.voice: The lines come right after ichhaa. In paraphrase: destroy all my enemies; save me with your own hand. May my family live in peace, and all my servants and Sikhs. A little later: protect me with your own hand, and end all my foes this very day. The word for enemy here is dusht, the wicked, the one who means harm. Sikhs read these lines in two ways, and they don't have to choose. The first is the plain one. The Guru and his community faced real violence, and this is a leader asking God to protect his people from those who would kill them. The tradition doesn't apologize for that; asking for protection from harm isn't hatred. The second goes inside. The Guru Granth Sahib speaks again and again of five thieves in every person: lust, anger, greed, attachment and ego. They live inside the body, the scripture says, and plunder its treasure. Many Sikhs, saying Chaupai every day, hear the enemies as those five too. The dusht that harms you most on an ordinary Tuesday probably isn't an army. It's your anger at the driver who cut you off, the greed that keeps you scrolling, the ego that can't say sorry. Notice where the prayer puts the fight. It doesn't say, let me destroy them. It says, you destroy them, and save me with your hand. The battle, inner or outer, is handed over. In the prayer's picture, the enemy within doesn't go because it's hated. It goes when the one praying is held by something stronger.
screen: `DESTROY MY ENEMIES; SAVE ME.` · `READING ONE: REAL ARMIES.` · `READING TWO: THE FIVE THIEVES.` · `YOU DESTROY THEM; HOLD ME.` · then, large: `END THE ENEMY WITHIN.`

segments.voice: Think of the five thieves, lust, anger, greed, attachment, ego, and without listing all your faults, notice which one has been busiest in you lately, and name it in one word. Then, instead of fighting it, picture handing it over, the way the prayer does. If you pray, say Waheguru as you do; if not, just let your grip on it loosen a little.
Dusht, the wicked. Chaupai's lines asking for enemies to be ended: real armies for the Guru, and for many Sikhs, the five thieves inside too.
Your line: end the enemy within. The fight, inner or outer, is handed over. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite these lines of Chaupai Sahib daily, understanding the enemies both as outward threats and as the five thieves: lust, anger, greed, attachment and ego.

what a scholar hears: by its traditional dating the poem comes from the years of tension around Anandpur, and Sikh commentary has long read its enemies on both levels, outward and inward.

notes: Verses paraphrased: 'hamre dusht sabhai tum ghaavahu, aap haath dai mohi bachaavahu; sukhee basai moro parivaaraa, sevak sikh sabhai kartaaraa' and 'mo rachhaa nij kar dai kariyai, sabh bairin ko aaj sanghariyai'. Confirm.

Historical setting: tensions with the hill rajas and later Mughal sieges of Anandpur, ending with the evacuation in 1704/1705. The voice keeps dates general ('the last years of the sixteen hundreds'). The trapdoor gives the traditional dating: Charitropakhyan's colophon is commonly given as 1753 Bikrami (1696 CE). Confirm.
Five thieves (kaam, krodh, lobh, moh, ahankar) and the image of thieves robbing the house: the Ang reference is a suggestion; Keeper to supply the best one.
Two readings presented as both held; confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): the five thieves no longer 'break in at night' (the scripture places them inside the body, plundering it; Ang 600, Sorath M3, is a likely reference); the closing claim about the enemy within is now framed as the prayer's picture, not narrator fact.
